career.line: Define what a useful finished version needs before polishing another detail.

relationship.line: Check whether repeated effort is answering the need that was actually expressed.

social.line: Join an activity for the experience rather than to demonstrate your ability.

questionPositions.situation: You may be concentrating on the work without checking whether the method still serves the purpose. Notice where repetition has become automatic or impossible to finish.
questionPositions.action: Choose one clear learning goal and a stopping point for this attempt. A useful practice includes time to review, not only time to repeat.
questionPositions.outcome: Reflect on how to recognise enough care without demanding a flawless result.

namedPersonPositions.you: You may be trying to get every gesture exactly right. Notice whether there is room to ask what is needed instead of guessing perfectly.
namedPersonPositions.them: Ask how the other person experiences the effort you are making. More work is not automatically the same as more useful care.
namedPersonPositions.connection: Consider whether a shared habit has become a task to complete rather than a choice to make. Bring attention back to its purpose.

upright.interpretation: You may have made room for something that suits your own taste and pace. Take a moment to appreciate it, and notice how your independence can coexist with welcome company.

career.line: Recognise a skill you can now use with greater independence.

relationship.line: Make space for your own interests alongside time together.

social.line: Choose company because you want it, rather than because you cannot enjoy time alone.

questionPositions.situation: You may be recognising the value of a practice or space you have shaped for yourself. Notice what allows you to enjoy it on your own terms.
questionPositions.action: Acknowledge the work behind what now feels familiar and choose how you want to use it. You do not need another person's approval to appreciate your own preference.
questionPositions.outcome: Consider what independence makes possible for you and what connection you still want to invite.

namedPersonPositions.you: You may value the room to make your own choices within this connection. Say which parts of your time or space matter to you.
namedPersonPositions.them: Ask what the other person enjoys doing independently. Their wish for their own space does not tell you how much they value time with you.
namedPersonPositions.connection: The connection may feel more spacious when neither person has to give up their own interests. Consider how chosen time together can sit alongside independence.

reversed.interpretation: Comparing your day with someone else's may make your own efforts difficult to recognise. Return to what you actually value and choose one ordinary pleasure that does not need to impress anyone.

career.line: Assess your work against its purpose rather than someone else's visible progress.

relationship.line: Notice whether you are asking the connection to prove your worth.

social.line: Choose a plan you enjoy without worrying how it appears to others.

questionPositions.situation: You may be measuring a personal achievement through standards that do not belong to you. Notice what you wanted from it before comparison entered the picture.
questionPositions.action: Name one thing you value for its own sake and give it a little attention. Review which expectations you actually want to keep.
questionPositions.outcome: Reflect on what enough would mean if the choice did not need an audience.

namedPersonPositions.you: You may be looking outside yourself for confirmation that you are doing this well. Notice which preference you can recognise without asking for agreement.
namedPersonPositions.them: Ask what the other person values instead of comparing yourself with an imagined standard. Their preferences need not become a measure of your worth.
namedPersonPositions.connection: Consider whether appearances are taking attention away from the experience between you. Discuss what feels worthwhile in private, ordinary moments.

upright.interpretation: A familiar practice may connect your day to people and efforts that came before it. Notice what you want to carry forward and how to make room for the people who belong here now.

career.line: Make a useful piece of knowledge easier for someone else to find.

relationship.line: Discuss which shared routines help you feel at home together.

social.line: Invite a newer person into a tradition without expecting them to know the rules.

questionPositions.situation: You may be working within an established group, routine or shared foundation. Notice what supports you and which expectations have never been openly discussed.
questionPositions.action: Preserve one useful practice and explain it clearly to someone taking part. Make room for their contribution to how it continues.
questionPositions.outcome: Consider what you would like your shared effort to make possible for the people who follow.

namedPersonPositions.you: You may be thinking about where this connection fits among your other ties and traditions. Name what belonging means to you in everyday terms.
namedPersonPositions.them: Ask which familiar practices matter to the other person. Their sense of home or belonging may have a different shape from yours.
namedPersonPositions.connection: The connection may be supported by the routines and communities around it. Consider which foundations you both want to keep and which need more room.

reversed.interpretation: An established way of doing things may no longer fit everyone involved. Notice which part still offers belonging and which expectation needs to be questioned or changed.

career.line: Question a long-standing process that excludes a useful contribution.

relationship.line: Separate a shared choice from an expectation inherited from other people.

social.line: Ask whether a familiar group ritual leaves enough room for different lives.

questionPositions.situation: You may be feeling a mismatch between an established arrangement and your present needs. Notice whether the difficulty lies in the practice itself or the pressure to accept it unchanged.
questionPositions.action: Name one expectation that needs discussion and suggest a practical alternative. A tradition can be valued without settling every present choice.
questionPositions.outcome: Reflect on what kind of belonging allows people to differ without having to leave their voice behind.

namedPersonPositions.you: You may be deciding which outside expectations belong in this connection. Notice what you would choose if those expectations were made explicit.
namedPersonPositions.them: Ask how the other person experiences the traditions or group expectations around you. Do not assume that a familiar background gives you the same priorities.
namedPersonPositions.connection: Consider what you want to define together rather than inherit unexamined. A shared foundation needs room for the people actually standing on it.

upright.interpretation: Something practical may be inviting you to become a beginner again. Give it a small, attentive attempt and notice what the experience teaches you beyond the idea of being good at it.

career.line: Try a new skill on a small task with room to ask questions.

relationship.line: Learn one everyday preference by asking rather than assuming.

social.line: Join an activity where curiosity matters more than experience.

questionPositions.situation: You may have an interest that needs hands-on experience before you can understand it well. Notice the simplest place to begin learning.
questionPositions.action: Choose a manageable exercise and ask for clear guidance where you need it. Record what you notice so the next attempt has something to build on.
questionPositions.outcome: Consider what you would enjoy learning if you allowed yourself to start without expertise.

namedPersonPositions.you: You may be curious about how to show up more thoughtfully here. Choose one practical question about what matters to the other person.
namedPersonPositions.them: Ask what the other person is interested in learning or trying. Leave room for their answer to be different from the role you imagined for them.
namedPersonPositions.connection: The connection may have room for learning something together. Choose a shared experiment small enough that neither person has to perform expertise.

reversed.interpretation: An idea may remain appealing while the practical first step keeps slipping away. Make that step smaller and clearer, then decide whether this is something you still want to give time to.

career.line: Turn a vague learning plan into one brief practice session.

relationship.line: Follow up on one small promise before offering another.

social.line: Choose one activity to try rather than collecting more possibilities.

questionPositions.situation: You may be gathering ideas without giving any of them a workable starting point. Notice whether you need a simpler task or a clearer reason to begin.
questionPositions.action: Set out the materials and the next action for one attempt. If your interest has changed, acknowledge that instead of building a larger plan.
questionPositions.outcome: Reflect on what would make learning part of your ordinary day rather than a distant intention.

namedPersonPositions.you: You may be thinking about a thoughtful gesture without making it concrete. Notice what you can actually do with the time you have.
namedPersonPositions.them: Ask what sort of follow-through the other person is comfortable offering. Enthusiasm alone does not establish an agreement.
namedPersonPositions.connection: Consider how to turn a shared intention into a modest, clear action. Keep the promise small enough for both people to understand it.

upright.interpretation: A steady approach may give an ordinary task the attention it needs. Keep the next step clear and manageable, while checking that the routine still serves the reason you began.

career.line: Complete one useful step carefully before adding more to the plan.

relationship.line: Follow through on an agreement in the way you actually discussed it.

social.line: Be clear and reliable about a plan without making it inflexible.

questionPositions.situation: You may be making progress through patient repetition rather than a dramatic change. Notice what the routine supports and what needs occasional review.
questionPositions.action: Choose the next practical step and give it a clear place in your day. Check the purpose as well as the completion of the task.
questionPositions.outcome: Consider what kind of consistency you can sustain without losing room to adapt.

namedPersonPositions.you: You may show care by being dependable in ordinary ways. Notice whether your reliability includes listening when the need changes.
namedPersonPositions.them: Ask what dependable support looks like to the other person. Their preferred rhythm may differ from the one that feels natural to you.
namedPersonPositions.connection: The connection may be shaped by promises that are small enough to keep. Consider how to make those promises clear and open to review.

reversed.interpretation: A dependable routine may be starting to feel more like an obligation than a choice. Review one part of it and decide whether a small change would bring the purpose back into view.

career.line: Change one repetitive step that no longer contributes to the result.

relationship.line: Ask whether an ordinary shared routine still feels good to both of you.

social.line: Suggest a small variation on a plan that has become automatic.

questionPositions.situation: You may be carrying on carefully without checking whether the approach still fits. Notice where consistency has become resistance to a useful change.
questionPositions.action: Review one recurring task against its purpose and adjust the part that no longer helps. You do not need to abandon the whole routine to make it more workable.
questionPositions.outcome: Reflect on what would let reliability include curiosity and responsiveness.

namedPersonPositions.you: You may be doing what has always been expected while feeling less present in it. Name the part you would like to change.
namedPersonPositions.them: Ask whether the other person still welcomes the familiar pattern. Repetition alone does not tell you whether it feels comforting or limiting to them.
namedPersonPositions.connection: Consider whether the connection needs a different rhythm rather than more effort at the same one. A small agreed change can be enough to explore.

upright.interpretation: Practical care may be close at hand in the way you arrange your time, space or attention. Notice what would make the day more welcoming for you as well as for anyone you care for.

career.line: Arrange your workspace so the next task is easier to begin.

relationship.line: Offer care that includes your own comfort and limits.

social.line: Make a shared space welcoming without taking responsibility for every detail.

questionPositions.situation: You may be noticing the ordinary conditions that help people feel comfortable and able to participate. Include your own needs in that picture.
questionPositions.action: Choose one practical improvement to the space, routine or task in front of you. Let it be useful without requiring you to attend to everything.
questionPositions.outcome: Consider what sustainable care looks like when the person offering it is included too.

namedPersonPositions.you: You may be expressing care through practical attention. Notice whether you are also allowing your own needs to be visible.
namedPersonPositions.them: Ask which everyday comforts matter to the other person. A caring intention becomes more specific when you hear their preference.
namedPersonPositions.connection: The connection may be supported by ordinary acts that make room for each other. Consider how both people can offer and receive that care.

reversed.interpretation: Attending to every practical need around you may leave your own day difficult to inhabit. Choose one task to share, simplify or leave, and make room for something that supports you.

career.line: Share a practical responsibility instead of quietly absorbing it.

relationship.line: Say what you need before taking on another act of care.

social.line: Let a gathering be simple enough that you can enjoy being part of it.

questionPositions.situation: You may be doing much of the work that makes a situation comfortable for others. Notice what that arrangement asks of you and whether it has been openly agreed.
questionPositions.action: Name one responsibility that needs sharing or simplifying. Make your own comfort a practical requirement rather than an optional extra.
questionPositions.outcome: Reflect on how care could become more sustainable without depending on you noticing everything first.

namedPersonPositions.you: You may have become the person who quietly makes things work. Notice which need you want to express rather than attend to alone.
namedPersonPositions.them: Ask what the other person can take responsibility for. They may need a clear conversation rather than another invisible act of preparation.
namedPersonPositions.connection: Consider how the practical work between you is recognised and shared. A comfortable connection should leave room for both people's needs.

upright.interpretation: Experience may help you make something useful and dependable today. Put it to work in a way that supports others' participation, while keeping the plan open to what they know.

career.line: Use your experience to make a process clearer for someone else.

relationship.line: Offer steady support without deciding the other person's priorities for them.

social.line: Help organise a shared plan while leaving room for others to shape it.

questionPositions.situation: You may be responsible for maintaining something that people rely on. Notice how your experience can provide support without becoming the only voice in the arrangement.
questionPositions.action: Make the practical requirements clear and invite others to take a meaningful part. Use what you know to support their judgement as well as the task.
questionPositions.outcome: Consider what dependable stewardship would leave stronger or easier for others to use.

namedPersonPositions.you: You may want to be someone the other person can rely on. Notice how to offer that steadiness without taking over their choices.
namedPersonPositions.them: Ask what support the other person values and what they prefer to manage themselves. Competence does not remove the need for consent.
namedPersonPositions.connection: The connection may benefit from dependable, shared foundations. Consider how responsibility can be held clearly without always belonging to the same person.

reversed.interpretation: A familiar way of keeping things orderly may be leaving too little room for other people's choices. Check which standards serve a real need and which mainly keep you in charge of the details.

career.line: Let someone use a different method if it meets the agreed need.

relationship.line: Offer practical help without making acceptance a condition of care.

social.line: Share the organising role instead of checking every detail yourself.

questionPositions.situation: You may be holding tightly to an arrangement because you know how to make it work. Notice whether that confidence is preventing other people from contributing their own judgement.
questionPositions.action: State the practical requirement and release control over a detail that does not affect it. Ask for a different view before defending the familiar method.
questionPositions.outcome: Reflect on how steadiness can include flexibility and shared responsibility.

namedPersonPositions.you: You may be equating care with making sure everything goes your way. Notice the part of the arrangement you could choose together instead.
namedPersonPositions.them: Ask how the other person wants to handle practical decisions. A different method does not tell you how seriously they take the connection.
namedPersonPositions.connection: Consider where control over details has replaced a shared agreement. Clear responsibilities can leave both people room to act in their own way.

suggestions: What deserves my focus at work?
How can I approach a difficult work conversation?
What could I learn from this next step?
career.lens: Read together, these cards invite you to consider your work through what is happening, what you can influence and what you hope to learn. Notice the part that belongs to your own choices, and one practical step that fits your capacity.

relationship.lens: Read together, these cards invite you to notice how you make room for closeness, boundaries and honest expression. Whether you are exploring a connection or reflecting on what you want, consider what you can say or choose without assuming how another person feels.

relationshipLenses.single: Read together, these cards invite you to consider what connection means to you while single. Notice the space you want for yourself, what draws you towards closeness and one choice that honours your own pace.
relationshipLenses.inRelationship: Read together, these cards invite you to reflect on the relationship you are in. Notice what you each bring, where a need could be named more clearly and one shared conversation that might make room for understanding.
relationshipLenses.complicated: Read together, these cards invite you to make room for uncertainty when a connection feels complicated. Notice what is clear to you, what remains unknown and one boundary or honest conversation that could help you find your own next step.

suggestions: How can I feel more connected to my friends?
What boundary would help me show up honestly?
What can I bring to this community?
social.lens: Read together, these cards invite you to reflect on belonging and the give and take between you and the people around you. Notice where a small gesture, a conversation or a boundary might make your connections feel more mutual.

reflections: What would you like to express more clearly?
What small choice would feel most honest to you now?
What are you noticing that you had not made room for before?
What would a kinder next step look like?
